response.answer: Power calculations for systemic outcomes like ΔCoVaR and expected systemic loss require determining minimum detectable effects and sample sizes, which depend on effect size, variance, and significance level. Simulation-based methods and tools like PUMP can estimate these parameters. Generally, larger sample sizes improve detection of small effects.

results.title: Power, Effect Sizes, and Minimum Detectable Effects
results.content: Power is sometimes also called “sensitivity.” Power refers to the ability of a test (i.e., an analysis of an experiment) to detect a “true effect” that is different from the null hypothesis (e.g., the ability to detect a difference between treatment and control when that difference actually exists). There are four factors that influence power: sample size, the true effect size, the variance of the effect, and the alpha-threshold (level of significance). If we have a more liberal threshold (i.e., a higher alpha level), we have more power to detect the effect. But this higher power is due to the fact that the more liberal treshold also increases our “false positive” rate, where the analysis is more likely to say there is an effect when in fact there is not. MDE tell us what is the smallest true effect, in standard deviations of the outcome, that is detectable for a given level of power and statistical significance.

# Decision Support A simulation-based method for estimating systemic risk measures. We propose a general simulation framework for estimating CoVaR, CoES and MES based on the asymptotic expansions. This paper focuses on simulation-based approaches for estimating systemic risk measures. In particular, we provide the asymptotic forms of the relative errors for widely used systemic risk measures including conditional value-at-risk (CoVaR), coexpected shortfall (CoES) and marginal expected shortfall (MES). Based on asymptotic expansions, a general framework is provided for the simulation of systemic risk measures. Systemic risk measures such as conditional value-at-risk (CoVaR)1, coexpected shortfall (CoES) and marginal expected shortfal (MES) were invented to evaluate the risk of one entity when another entity is under distress. In the model-based approaches, the data used in practical application needs to satisfy model assumptions, and different methods for estimating systemic risk measures are required under different models. However, the application of simulation methods to systemic risk measures is rare. First, the simulation time for estimating systemic risk measures increases several fold as the dimensions increase from one to two, resulting in inefficient estimation. The relative error and required sample size can be obtained directly by calculating simple factors with these asymptotic expansions, which facilitates controlling the estimation error when simulating systemic risk measures. We provide the asymptotic forms for the relative errors for widely used systemic risk measures including CoVaR, CoES and MES. We propose a general simulation framework for estimating CoVaR, CoES and MES based on the asymptotic expansions for relative errors. In simulating systemic risk measures, it is unreasonable to estimate an estimator without evaluating its accuracy. In this paper, we introduce a simulation-based method for estimating systemic risk measures. Based on these asymptotic expansions, Algorithm 2 provides a general framework for simulating systemic risk measures. ### Systemic risk measurement: Multivariate GARCH estimation of covar. The CoVaR and CoES are two of the most widely used measures of systemic risk in economics and finance. This method extends existing Asymmetric Laplace (AL) joint estimation techniques for Value at Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES) to the realm of systemic risk measures.

results.title: Optimal Design of Cluster- and Multisite-Randomized Studies Using Fallible Outcome Measures - Kyle Cox, Benjamin Kelcey, 2019
results.content: We develop simple formulas to adjust statistical power, minimum detectable effect (MDE), and optimal sample allocation formulas for two-level cluster- and multisite-randomized designs when the outcome is subject to measurement error. Next, we incorporate measurement error into the outcome of the analytic model and develop formulas for the error variance of the treatment effect and each design consideration (i.e., power, MDE, optimal sample allocation) that accounts for this error. Percent of Change in Power and Minimum Detectable Effect (MDE) Due to Measurement Error in the Outcome for Two-Level Cluster-Randomized Trials Under the Optimal Sample Allocation Framework. Ignoring this additional variance will have detrimental effects on the accuracy of design considerations (e.g., power, MDE, optimal sample allocation) when planning MSRTs. The σδ formulation for MSRTs suggests that directly reduces the detrimental influence of measurement error in the outcome at Level 1 and indirectly addresses measurement error and its additional variance as a divisor of the entire error variance of the treatment effect expression. This work developed expression directed toward two objectives: (a) the development of simple and accessible expressions of statistical power, MDE, and optimal sample allocation that help plan for the undermining effects of measurement error in two-level cluster- and multisite-randomized designs and (b) the subsequent investigation of these expressions to assess the nature and scope of the detrimental effects of measurement error on planning these multilevel experiments. In general, measurement error in the Level 1 outcome of these designs reduced power, increased the MDE, and inflated optimal individual sample size. results.content: Thus, if the test of the treatment effect would have required a sample size of *N* subjects for a given level of power under classic conditions, the fact that subjects are clustered increases the needed sample size to approximately *DN*. We chose to center time despite this disadvantage, because the expression *Ytij* = *π*0*ij* + *π*1*ij**Ttij* + *etij* with random effects in *π*1*ij* forces the cluster-level error variance to depend on the magnitude of *T*, so that (without further *ad hoc* changes to the parameterization) a 0/1 coding would have required making the strong assumption that cluster-level error variance is considerably higher at posttest than at pretest, and this limitation would have made it more difficult to provide useful power formulas. We use Monte Carlo simulations to explore (a) whether it is feasible to obtain acceptable statistical power for detecting main effects and two-way interactions in a screening experiment, using multilevel factorial designs with sample sizes commonly available in practice; and (b) how adequately the power formulas proposed here for within- and between-clusters factorial designs, can predict power. Table 5 shows the simulated power, along with Type I error rates, for main effects in within-clusters experiments under different conditions of ICC, *J* and *n̄*. The simulation results indicate that under reasonable scenarios of number of clusters, number of individuals within clusters, and ICC, it is often possible to conduct a multifactor factorial experiment with adequate power for detecting main effects, even when the population of interest is multilevel. As expected, within-clusters assignment offered better power than between-clusters assignment, but results suggest that under certain conditions it is possible to obtain excellent power for main effects in a between-clusters factorial design. Most of the findings in the simulations agreed with past literature, but one seems initially surprising:the *increase* in Type I error rate with *higher* sample sizes (*J* or *n̄*) in fractional factorial designs. Because such studies are often aimed at testing interactions or comparing individual cells rather than testing main effects, the required sample size for detecting the effects of interest is likely to be very large, especially for between-clusters factorial designs (Murray, 1998; Donner & Klar,2000).
